comparison: Perfect agreement on behavioral findings (C2-C6). Both evaluations support these claims without critique. OpenEval emphasizes statistical rigor and appropriate interpretation of marginal effects, while peer reviewers treat these as established observations that the new model explains.

Perfect agreement on null learning rate findings (C12, C19, C20). Both strongly support this as a central contribution. OpenEval frames it as a theoretically important negative result, while peer reviewers describe it as 'remarkable' evidence that 'calls into question a class of existing models.'

Perfect agreement on simulation results (C13-C15). Both support these findings as part of comprehensive model validation. OpenEval emphasizes the mechanistic explanation, while peer reviewers accept these as part of exploring why the new model is superior.

Perfect agreement on clinical correlations (C16-C18). Both support these findings as clinically relevant. OpenEval notes moderate effect sizes and theoretical coherence, while peer reviewers endorse this as a key contribution but caution about small sample size limitations.

Perfect agreement on simulation demonstration (C21-C23). Both strongly support this as critical evidence. OpenEval notes methodological soundness and potential confounding between model interpretations, while peer reviewers treat this as 'remarkable' validation of theoretical claims.

Perfect agreement on main conclusions (C49-C52). Both strongly endorse these interpretive claims. OpenEval notes appropriate framing acknowledging correlational evidence, while peer reviewers provide 'convincing support' and emphasize the novel perspective on learning effects.

Strong agreement on theoretical framework (C34-C37) and model selection (C7-C8). OpenEval supports model fit metrics but suggests additional justification needed for strategy choices. Peer reviewers strongly endorse the theoretical framework as a 'novel and valuable alternative explanation' and major contribution.

Strong agreement on model validation (C24-C26). Both praise the rigorous parameter and model recovery analyses. OpenEval emphasizes this addresses concerns about model confounding, while peer reviewers unanimously praise the 'rigorously conducted parameter retrieval' and sophisticated methods.

Agreement on experimental design (C27-C33 overlap with C1, C27-C33). Both support the task design and methods. OpenEval notes good retention with minor selection effects, while peer reviewers accept the design noting it's a reanalysis of published data with one limitation about uncertainty differentiation for future work.

Partial overlap on participant recruitment methods (C53-C57). OpenEval supports the diagnostic procedures but notes heterogeneity from inconsistent SCID use. Peer reviewers praise overall methodological rigor but note small clinical sample size as a limitation for interpreting clinical results.

Partial overlap on parameter estimation methods (C65, C72-C74). OpenEval supports the MAP approach but notes missing details on convergence criteria and prior specifications. Peer reviewers explicitly praise 'appropriate and sophisticated methods' for parameterizing and fitting the model.

Partial overlap on data/code availability (C75-C76). OpenEval supports the transparency statements noting they enable reproducibility. Peer reviewers implicitly endorse this through overall positive assessment of methodological rigor, with explicit praise for 'rigorously conducted' work.

OpenEval evaluated literature review claims (C38-C45) as accurately summarizing prior work with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these literature summary claims.

OpenEval evaluated critiques of traditional approaches (C46-C48) as valid concerns about overfitting, assumptions, and observability. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these methodological critique claims, though peer reviewers endorsed the overall alternative approach.
